title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space

paper.title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have become the dominant framework for high-fidelity image generation by progressively refining noise into structured samples. [ 5 , 30 , 23 ] However, this strong generation quality comes at the cost of iterative denoising across many timesteps, making sampling inherently sequential and limiting throughput. 1 1 1 Throughput = images generated total inference time = images per forward pass inference time per forward pass \mathrm{Throughput}=\frac{\text{images generated}}{\text{total inference time}}=\frac{\text{images per forward pass}}{\text{inference time per forward pass}} . Prior work has made substantial progress by reducing the per-sample cost of diffusion sampling. One line of work reduces the number of denoising evaluations. [ 30 , 31 , 27 , 12 , 13 , 38 , 40 , 39 ] Another line of work reduces the cost of individual denoising evaluations through feature reuse or caching. [ 14 , 8 ] Together, these approaches have substantially improved the efficiency–quality trade-off of diffusion sampling in practice. Despite these advances, further acceleration along the same per-sample axis is increasingly difficult. As denoising evaluations decrease, each remaining step must approximate more of the trajectory, making the dynamics more sensitive to approximation error. [ 34 , 35 ] Caching methods reuse intermediate features across adjacent timesteps, but wider cache intervals amplify mismatch from fully recomputed trajectories. [ 14 ] When the two approaches are combined, reduced-step sampling makes each update more consequential while caching supplies features from increasingly mismatched trajectory states, limiting further gains without additional quality loss overall. Figure 1: Illustration of the ManiFusion framework. K × B K\times B inputs is fused into B B representations, jointly processed by a shared denoising backbone, then unfused via the unfusion module into K K representations per group, and finally passed through a projection layer to produce K K outputs. As gains along the per-sample axis approach saturation, we instead increase throughput by processing more samples within each denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion , a lightweight framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion processes multiple samples within a shared denoising backbone by fusing their representations before the backbone and separating them afterward through index-conditioned unfusion. Specifically, ManiFusion realizes multi-sample computation through Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which uses larger fusion factors in stable regions and smaller factors in sensitive stages. However, generating multiple samples through a single fused representation presents a nontrivial challenge. Each sample needs a distinct denoising prediction, yet fusion combines their states into a representation the size of a single input. Naive superposition can entangle their information [ 37 , 33 ] and compromise the denoising dynamics governing their individual generation trajectories. [ 30 , 9 ] We examine how shared computation can preserve these distinct predictions through a geometric perspective under the manifold hypothesis. [ 20 , 28 , 1 , 2 ] Low-dimensional data structure provides room for samples to coexist, while denoising requires their prediction targets to remain recoverable. Our analysis relates fusion-induced information loss to prediction error, supported by empirical studies of sample separation and denoising behavior. To demonstrate that ManiFusion generalizes across diverse generative settings, we validate ManiFusion across major diffusion model families, including pixel-space U-Nets, diffusion transformers, and latent diffusion models. [ 24 , 22 , 23 ] Our experiments cover both unconditional and conditional generation across broad resolution ranges from CIFAR-10 to ImageNet. We further show that ManiFusion composes naturally with existing acceleration methods, including step-reduction samplers and caching-based acceleration. [ 12 , 31 , 14 ] By operating along a different throughput axis, ManiFusion reaches higher-throughput regimes beyond trajectory shortening or per-step acceleration alone.

sections.heading: 2 Method
sections.text: We propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. Since multi-sample generation requires jointly processing multiple trajectories while preserving sample-wise prediction targets, we first establish ManiFusion through dual-space inference (Sec. 2.1 ). In this framework, multiple denoising evaluations are replaced by a single fused computation followed by index-conditioned recovery. We then extend ManiFusion across diverse diffusion backbones and sampling paradigms through Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically allocates the fusion factor according to trajectory dynamics (Sec. 2.2 ). Finally, we develop a geometric intuition for why shared computation can support distinct generation trajectories and what information fusion must preserve to make this possible (Sec. 2.3 ).

sections.heading: Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling.
sections.text: For these denoiser-level variants, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which allocates the fusion factor according to the local behavior of the generative trajectory. This is motivated by the observation that the approximation quality in Eq. 3 varies throughout the diffusion process, since the stability of dual-space computation depends on the local trajectory behavior. We therefore define the fusion factor K t = κ ⁡ ( t ) K_{t}=\kappa(t) as a function of timestep t t . At each timestep, samples are grouped into tuples of size K t K_{t} , and fused computation is applied to each group as z t = F K t ​ ( x t 1 , … , x t K t ) z_{t}=F_{K_{t}}(x_{t}^{1},\dots,x_{t}^{K_{t}}) and ( y ^ t 1 , … , y ^ t K t ) = U K t ​ ( f ~ t , K t ​ ( z t ) ) (\hat{y}_{t}^{1},\dots,\hat{y}_{t}^{K_{t}})=U_{K_{t}}(\tilde{f}_{t,K_{t}}(z_{t})) . By allocating fusion factors according to trajectory dynamics, ManiFusion balances computational efficiency and sample fidelity across denoising stages without changing the backbone.

sections.heading: 2.2 Instantiation Across Architectures and Generative Flows
sections.text: To examine whether fused computation generalizes across model designs, we instantiate ManiFusion in U-Nets, diffusion transformers, and autoencoders, covering convolutional and attention-based backbones as well as denoiser-level and latent-representation sharing. We further consider DDPM, DDIM, and Flow Matching to study how this principle applies across different generative dynamics.

sections.heading: Backbone restructuring
sections.text: To maximize shared computation across multiple trajectories, ManiFusion restructures the denoiser such that most computation is performed in the fused space. Let ℬ \mathcal{B} denote the heavy backbone body of the denoiser and ℋ \mathcal{H} its final projection head. Instead of repeatedly evaluating ℬ \mathcal{B} for each trajectory independently, ManiFusion places the fusion module F F before ℬ \mathcal{B} and the unfusion module U U after ℬ \mathcal{B} , allowing the dominant backbone computation to be shared across fused trajectories. sections.heading: MF-UNet
sections.text: For pixel-space models such as DDPM, we split the U-Net at its final convolutional layer, treating the multi-scale convolutional backbone as the shared body and the output convolution as the head. Fusion uses lightweight 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutional blocks per index, while unfusion uses pointwise convolutions. Because the body output already encodes rich spatial features [ 24 ] , simple channel-wise separation suffices without modifying the U-Net internals.

sections.heading: MF-DiT
sections.text: For transformer-based models such as DiT, inputs have shape B × K × L × d B\times K\times L\times d , where L L is the number of patch tokens. To treat the whole transformer stack as the shared body, we split the denoiser at the final linear projection. Fusion and unfusion are implemented as index-conditioned fully connected layers applied identically across patch positions ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } \ell\in\{1,\dots,L\} , sharing parameters to preserve token-wise structure and permutation sensitivity across all patch tokens.

sections.heading: MF-AE
sections.text: For latent diffusion models, fusion is applied at the representation level of the autoencoder rather than within the denoising trajectory. We extend ManiFusion by inserting fusion before encoding and unfusion after decoding, effectively operating on a shared latent representation. During autoencoder training, multiple inputs are fused prior to encoding and reconstructed through a shared latent. At generation time, a shared latent is denoised and decoded jointly. Unfusion is then applied at the output to recover individual samples. Because fusion operates at the representation level, K K remains fixed during sampling.

sections.heading: Trajectory-dependent fusion allocation
sections.text: To show that trajectory-dependent fusion naturally generalizes across both score-based diffusion and velocity-based generative flows, we apply TFS by switching between independently trained fixed- K K models during inference. For DDPM, larger fusion factors are assigned to early noisy stages and smaller factors to later stages, consistent with the coarse-to-fine behavior of diffusion trajectories [ 6 , 35 ] . Specifically, we allocate 50% of timesteps to K = 4 K{=}4 , 25% to K = 2 K{=}2 , and 25% to K = 1 K{=}1 . 2 2 2 This yields an idealized 2 × 2\times throughput since the effective cost is 1 4 × 0.5 + 1 2 × 0.25 + 1 × 0.25 = 0.5 \tfrac{1}{4}\times 0.5+\tfrac{1}{2}\times 0.25+1\times 0.25=0.5 . DDIM [ 30 ] uses the same allocation. For Flow Matching [ 9 ] , we instead assign larger fusion factors to regions with smaller scheduler intervals, where the same velocity prediction error contributes a smaller displacement error to each update (Sec. 2.3 ). Finally, we combine ManiFusion with step-reduction samplers and per-step acceleration methods such as DeepCache [ 14 ] , achieving additional throughput gains with only slight quality degradation.

sections.heading: 2.3 Geometric Analysis
sections.text: Fusing multiple samples reduces computation, but how can a single shared representation support the distinct predictions needed to generate each sample? To answer this question, we examine which differences between inputs must remain distinguishable after fusion for their predictions to be recovered. The low-dimensional structure of clean data provides a geometric basis for preserving these distinctions within a shared space. We then extend this reasoning to noisy inputs, where the information needed for prediction changes along the denoising trajectory, motivating adaptive allocation of shared computation.

sections.heading: Noisy targets and trajectory-dependent allocation.
sections.text: The clean-manifold argument concerns the K ​ d Kd intrinsic coordinates of a clean tuple. sections.heading: Diffusion Models and Baselines.
sections.text: Our goal is to validate ManiFusion as a general computational restructuring principle that operates across diverse generative settings, rather than a technique specialized to a particular pretrained foundation model stack. We therefore evaluate ManiFusion across major diffusion model families spanning different denoising spaces, backbone architectures, and conditional generation settings. For pixel-space U-Nets, we apply MF-UNet to DDPM [ 5 ] on CIFAR-10 and CelebA. For pixel-space transformers and conditional generation, we evaluate MF-DiT on class-conditional DiT [ 22 ] on CIFAR-10. For latent-space autoencoders, we apply MF-AE to LDM [ 23 ] on CelebA-HQ. Finally, for latent-space transformers and conditional generation, we evaluate MF-DiT on ImageNet using DiT [ 22 ] . These experiments demonstrate that ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion model families rather than specific architectures, scaling across resolutions, denoising spaces, and conditioning regimes.

sections.heading: Experimental settings.
sections.text: All throughput measurements are conducted using batched inference for vanilla baselines and ManiFusion under identical inference environments, including sufficiently large batch configurations, scheduler settings, and hardware setup, to ensure fair comparison. Throughput is reported using end-to-end wall-clock generation time, and computational overhead is evaluated using parameter count and multiply–accumulate operations (MACs). Unless otherwise specified, all ManiFusion results use fusion factors up to K=4, and all models are trained from scratch without finetuning or freezing. Additional details and ablations appear in the appendix.

sections.text: We first evaluate ManiFusion on baseline diffusion models, where it achieves nearly 2 × \times throughput while maintaining sample quality close to the baseline without materially increasing model complexity(Tab. 1 ). Interestingly, mixing different class conditions within fused groups is more stable than grouping identical classes, as verified by additional experiments in the Appendix. This supports the interpretation that conditional diversity provides cues for slot separation (Appendix C ). We extend ManiFusion to latent diffusion in two ways. MF-AE learns a representation for joint reconstruction, whereas MF-UNet shares the prediction computation at each denoising step. We further evaluate MF-DiT on ImageNet for large-scale class-conditional generation. These results show strong quality across latent U-Net and transformer backbones in both settings. sections.heading: 3.2 Orthogonal Acceleration Beyond Existing Throughput Limits
sections.text: We extend ManiFusion to step-reduction frameworks, demonstrating that per-step multi-sample acceleration is complementary to trajectory shortening. As shown in Fig. 2 , ManiFusion maintains higher sample quality at matched throughput. In contrast, baseline methods rapidly degrade beyond their practical throughput ceiling, highlighting the advantage of trajectory-dependent fusion allocation in high-throughput regimes. Finally, we combine ManiFusion with DeepCache to demonstrate compatibility with caching-based acceleration. At matched throughput, the combined approach consistently outperforms configurations relying solely on step-reduction and caching(Tab. 2 ). These results suggest that compressing computation along a single axis is fundamentally limited, whereas combining orthogonal acceleration strategies yields compounding efficiency gains in high-throughput settings.

sections.heading: 4 Analysis
sections.text: Figure 3: Analysis of the representation geometry induced by ManiFusion. (a) Geometric diagnostics measure prediction separation using response-distance ratios, and vector-field consistency and dynamics alignment using cosine similarity. (b) Training dynamics of Fusion Weight Orthogonality for MF-AE with K = 4 K=4 , showing the development of slot-specific separation during training. We analyze the geometry and dynamics induced by multiplexed generation under ManiFusion. In particular, we study whether fusion preserves distinguishability, maintains consistent generative dynamics, and develops stable separation during training. To this end, we examine prediction separation, vector-field consistency, dynamics alignment, and fusion-module behavior. Additional visualizations and toy analysis on the D ≥ K ​ d D\geq Kd condition are provided in the appendix.

sections.heading: 4.1 Empirical Validation of the Geometric Analysis
sections.text: To examine whether fusion retains prediction-relevant distinctions (Sec. 2.3 ), we compare velocity-prediction distances with those of the single-sample model. Figure 3 (a) reports their ratios for same-class local perturbations and random tuple pairs. Ratios near one indicate comparable prediction separation. The random-pair ratios concentrate near one, whereas local ratios shift downward as K K increases. Fusion thus preserves broad prediction differences while attenuating finer distinctions under stronger compression. The Appendix further examines local sensitivity. Sharing a representation also requires compatible predictions. To examine this requirement, we compare slot-wise vector-field directions between complete tuples. Collision pairs have nearby fused representations, approximating a shared fiber, while non-collision pairs are farther apart. Near-fiber pairs exhibit higher cosine similarity over much of the trajectory, indicating a relative tendency toward more compatible field directions. To connect this agreement to generation, we also assess alignment with the reference dynamics. Alignment with the single-sample model remains close to one in early stages but declines near the end, particularly for K = 8 K=8 . These results motivate TFS, which shares more computation early and restores sample-specific capacity during final refinement. Schedule ablations evaluate the quality–throughput trade-off.

sections.heading: 4.2 Training Dynamics of the Fusion Module
sections.text: To further understand the fusion mechanism, we analyze the training dynamics of the fusion module through Fusion Weight Orthogonality , defined as the average squared inner product between normalized fusion weight vectors. Figure 3 shows that the value initially increases and then decreases after approximately 50 ​ k 50\mathrm{k} steps. Early in training, different streams produce nearly identical faces, and separation emerges progressively as individual streams diverge in structure. Once the generated images begin to exhibit distinct color patterns across streams, Fusion Weight Orthogonality starts to decrease, indicating that the fusion weight vectors become increasingly orthogonal. This suggests that the fusion module gradually reorganizes its parameter space to allocate independent slot-specific directions for different samples, supporting the trajectory-wise separation discussed in Sec. 2.3 .

sections.heading: Diffusion Models
sections.text: Diffusion models have become a dominant class of generative models by learning to iteratively denoise corrupted signals [ 29 , 5 , 32 ] . Pixel-space approaches such as DDPM operate directly in image space [ 5 ] , while Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) perform denoising in compressed but still high-capacity latent space [ 23 ] . Recent transformer-based variants such as DiT [ 22 ] demonstrate that larger latent representations and L/XL-scale backbones improve performance but also increase inference cost. Across these formulations, diffusion models leave substantial representational slack for ManiFusion, increasing the potential of fused multi-sample computation at scale.

sections.heading: Diffusion Model Acceleration
sections.text: The primary bottleneck of diffusion models is iterative inference, where generating a single sample requires many sequential denoising steps and repeated network evaluations. A large body of work therefore focuses on reducing the number of sampling steps. For example, DDIM reformulates the reverse process with fewer iterations [ 30 , 18 ] , while flow-matching methods learn continuous-time vector fields that directly transport noise to data [ 9 , 10 ] . Another line of work reduces the cost of each sampling step through caching. Methods such as DeepCache and CacheMe reuse intermediate activations across timesteps to avoid redundant computation and lower per-step latency. [ 19 , 34 , 36 ] However, these approaches still process each trajectory independently and therefore do not improve multi-sample throughput within a single denoising evaluation.

sections.heading: Superposition in Deep Learning
sections.text: A line of work has explored accelerating neural networks by superposing multiple inputs into a shared representation. For example, the Byte Latent Transformer [ 21 ] leverages sparsity to process groups of tokens jointly, while Latent Attention [ 11 ] fuses multiple tokens into a shared latent representation for attention. Liu.al. [ 16 ] extended input superposition to sentence- and token-level classification, while Menet et al. [ 15 ] applied the concept to the classification of small-scale image datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10. In contrast, we are the first to apply superposition to generative modeling by fusing multiple signals within a latent trajectory, allowing one inference process to generate multiple images without quality loss.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we proposed ManiFusion, a diffusion acceleration framework that improves throughput by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. Rather than relying only on trajectory shortening or per-step latency reduction, ManiFusion introduces a complementary throughput axis by increasing the number of samples processed per evaluation. Our geometric analysis explains how shared representations can retain sample-wise prediction information, while trajectory-aware fusion allocation balances throughput and generation quality. Across diverse diffusion settings, ManiFusion operates on top of existing acceleration strategies and enables throughput regimes difficult to achieve with them alone. These results position ManiFusion as a scalable direction for future diffusion acceleration.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: A limitation of ManiFusion is that it currently requires full pretraining to integrate fused computation into the denoising backbone, resulting in substantial computational cost and preventing lightweight finetuning-based adaptation. In addition, we do not evaluate large-scale text-to-image foundation models, limiting our study to discussing potential scalability rather than empirically validating such settings. Finally, performance can still degrade under extreme fusion factors, suggesting remaining limits in high-throughput scaling.

sections.heading: Appendix A Appendix Overview
sections.text: This appendix follows the main paper from implementation to analysis and evaluation. We first provide training and inference configurations, followed by derivations supporting the geometric analysis. We then examine clean-manifold capacity, local sensitivity, interpolation, and feature-space coverage empirically. Next come extensions through larger fusion factors, TFS, DeepCache, and latent diffusion, followed by conditional grouping and kernel-size ablations. We conclude with throughput-oriented baseline comparisons and qualitative results organized by sampler, throughput, and latent fusion design.

sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation Details
sections.text: We describe here the training and inference configurations and metric informations used across all datasets and model families.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: We assess perceptual quality and distributional coverage along five complementary axes. First, Inception Score (IS) [ 26 ] and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 4 ] to jointly capture sample diversity and global visual fidelity. Second, we compute the spatial FID (sFID), which measures the Fréchet distance over intermediate feature maps that preserve spatial structure, providing a more sensitive evaluation of local detail and geometric fidelity [ 17 , 3 ] . We additionally report precision and recall [ 7 , 25 ] to quantify manifold fidelity and coverage under fusion. Moreover, all Macs, Throughputs are measured by a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU with batched inference of batch 128.

sections.heading: Configurations
sections.text: For CIFAR-10 DDPM, we follow the protocol of Ho et al. [ 5 ] , while CelebA DDPM and the DDIM samplers adopt the settings of Song et al. [ 30 ] . For Flow Matching on CIFAR-10, we replicate Lipman et al. [ 10 ] . For CelebA, no official baseline exists, so we define its configuration consistently with the rest of our experiments. For latent diffusion models, we follow the training and sampling setup of Rombach et al. [ 23 ] . For transformer-based diffusion models, we adopt the DiT configuration proposed by Peebles and Xie [ 22 ] for ImageNet. Across all experiments, models are trained with a fixed fusion factor K K . Each model is trained independently for its corresponding K K , and no mixture of fusion factors is used during training. The index embeddings used for demultiplexing are therefore defined only for the corresponding K K and remain fixed throughout training and inference. We do not introduce additional regularization or curriculum strategies. Separation emerges from the architecture and training objective. For Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling(TFS), we combine models trained with different fusion factors during inference. The denoising trajectory is partitioned into intervals and each interval uses the model trained with the corresponding K K . This allows large fusion factors in early timesteps for higher throughput while gradually reducing K K later to preserve generation quality. For the denoiser-level variants, TFS switches among independently trained fixed- K K predictors while the sampler retains the individual sample states. Each selected predictor supplies slot-wise update targets as in Eq. 12 . Changing K K therefore changes the amount of shared prediction computation while preserving the sample-wise sampling interface. We use trajectory stage for DDPM/DDIM and scheduler intervals for Flow Matching to allocate this computation. The latter choice follows the step-size scaling in Eq. 23 . Schedule ablations measure the resulting quality–throughput trade-off. MF-AE uses a fixed K K throughout shared-latent generation and unfuses after decoding. Across all cases, the same learning rate schedule, noise schedule, and sampling procedure are maintained for each fixed- K K model. Evaluation is performed on 50k generated samples using the implementation of Dhariwal et al. [ 3 ] , ensuring that any performance differences can be attributed solely to the ManiFusion modules. sections.heading: Appendix C Derivations for the Geometric Analysis
sections.text: We analyze fusion through the information required for prediction. The central principle is that complete tuples mapped to the same fused representation should require compatible prediction targets. Clean-manifold capacity, fiber-wise consistency at noisy timesteps, and trajectory-dependent fusion allocation are different aspects of this principle. The timestep-wise analysis concerns MF-UNet and MF-DiT. The clean-reconstruction argument also describes the representation bottleneck of MF-AE. The risk decomposition establishes the prediction criterion. The geometric arguments explain how representation capacity and separation support it. The experiments then examine these mechanisms in learned models.

sections.heading: Conditional grouping and slot separation.
sections.text: Fiber consistency compares different complete tuples mapped to a shared representation. Conditional grouping determines how the individual slots within each tuple can be separated by unfusion. Diverse class conditions supply additional cues for assigning predicted features to the appropriate slot. The benefit of mixed-condition grouping therefore complements compatibility across tuples. One concerns slot separation, while the other concerns shared prediction behavior. Same-condition samples retain distinct noisy states and targets, providing alternative cues for unfusion. Our class-conditional grouping experiment examines how the availability of these cues affects generation quality.

sections.heading: Scope of the analysis.
sections.text: The identities above describe fixed-timestep population risk under squared loss, and the clean-capacity argument assumes smooth maps on the clean manifold. The empirical analyses use learned reference fields and finite perturbations to examine the associated prediction geometry. End-to-end generation quality and the cumulative effects of fusion are assessed by the sampling metrics and TFS ablations.

sections.heading: Toy experiment
sections.text: To empirically validate the proposed geometric analysis, we construct a controlled setting in which the intrinsic dimension d d and ambient dimension D D are explicitly separated. Latent samples x ^ ∈ ℝ d \hat{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are drawn from a low-dimensional distribution and embedded into the ambient space ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} through a fixed column-orthogonal projection P ∈ ℝ D × d P\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d} satisfying P ⊤ ​ P = I P^{\top}P=I , yielding observations x = P ​ x ^ x=P\hat{x} . The projection is unknown to the model, so diffusion models are trained entirely in the ambient space using lightweight MLP denoisers. To inspect the intrinsic structure, generated samples are projected back to the latent coordinates through P ⊤ P^{\top} . Within this setting, we train denoisers both with and without fusion and analyze the resulting fused dynamics under different fusion factors. To examine clean-manifold capacity under fusion, we vary the relationship between the ambient dimension D D and the fused intrinsic dimension K ​ d Kd . Consistent with the necessary capacity condition derived in Sec. 2.3 , recovery fails when the ambient space cannot represent the fused product manifold, while stable separation is observed for D ≥ K ​ d D\geq Kd in the evaluated configurations (Fig. 4 ). This transition empirically supports the role of representation capacity in clean-sample recovery. To examine representation alignment, we analyze the geometry induced by the fusion map in the ambient denoising space. We visualize fused representations after projection to the intrinsic coordinates through P ⊤ P^{\top} . Although the fused geometry does not initially coincide with the single-sample manifold, an affine alignment in the ambient space substantially reduces the discrepancy. In recoverable regimes, the aligned fused geometry closely matches the single-sample manifold structure, supporting preservation of the reference structure in the projected features. sections.heading: Conditional Grouping and Intra-Tuple Separability
sections.text: We analyze how conditional grouping affects the separability of fused samples in MF-DiT. During training, fused inputs can be constructed either by grouping samples that share the same condition or by randomly mixing conditions within a fusion group. Table 9 shows that random condition mixing consistently outperforms uni-class grouping. This observation supports the interpretation that conditional diversity provides clearer slot-specific cues and eases index-conditioned unfusion. This is an intra-tuple separation effect, whereas fiber consistency concerns compatibility between predictions for different complete tuples sharing a fused representation. Same-condition grouping remains effective in the evaluated setting because individual trajectories still have distinct noisy states and targets, although fewer condition-specific cues can make separation harder. sections.heading: Comparison with a Naive Patch-Based Baseline.
sections.text: We first compare ManiFusion with a naive patch-based strategy that attempts to increase throughput by spatially compositing multiple inputs. Using the same model architectures and dataset configurations described in Section B , we design a naive multi-sample strategy where each noisy input is first downscaled to one-quarter resolution, concatenated into a 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid, processed once by the diffusion model, and then split and upscaled back to full resolution. This simple approach, however, severely degrades generation quality. As illustrated in Table 11 , the patch-based method introduces artifacts, unnatural boundaries, and facial/background blur, while ManiFusion preserves texture and color consistency. Quantitative results in Table 12 further confirm this gap. When applied to a standard DDPM, the patch-based method suffers a dramatic quality drop—on CIFAR-10, FID deteriorates from 18.27 (ManiFusion) to 91.71, and IS falls from 7.41 to 4.55. On CelebA, ManiFusion achieves an FID of 9.50 versus 26.07 for the grid approach, and an IS of 2.58 compared to 2.37. These findings demonstrate that our fusion–unfusion modules not only preserve and disentangle multi-sample information more effectively than naive patch compositing but also scale reliably to higher throughput settings. Together, the qualitative and quantitative evidence underscores the scalability of ManiFusion and its potential to unlock further efficiency gains without compromising visual fidelity. sections.heading: Comparison with Capacity-Reduced Models.
sections.text: Beyond comparisons to naive compositing, we also evaluate whether ManiFusion simply mimics the effect of reducing model size to improve throughput. To this end, we construct two reduced-computation U-Net variants trained on CIFAR-10 at K = 2 K=2 . The first is a channel-reduced model, which decreases the number of feature maps per layer by modifying the channel multipliers. The second is a depth-reduced model, which shortens the network depth by removing residual blocks. These variants allow us to compare shared computation with reductions in backbone capacity at comparable computational budgets. Detailed configurations are listed in Table 13 , and quantitative results are reported in Table 14 . The reference in this comparison is ManiFusion with the full backbone at K = 2 K=2 . Both reduced models require more MACs and achieve lower throughput than this reference. FID increases from 5.93 for ManiFusion to 7.59 for the channel-reduced model and 6.55 for the depth-reduced model, with corresponding declines in IS and recall. This comparison distinguishes two ways of reducing per-sample computation. Smaller backbones reduce the capacity used to process inputs, whereas ManiFusion shares the computation of the full backbone across multiple samples. In the tested configurations, the latter achieves better quality at lower MAC counts and higher throughput. These results support retaining backbone capacity through fusion as an effective alternative to reducing channels or depth. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation. 1 Introduction Diffusion models have become the dominant framework for high-fidelity image generation by progressively refining noise into structured samples. [ 5 , 30 , 23 ] However, this strong generation quality comes at the cost of iterative denoising across many timesteps, making sampling inherently sequential and limiting throughput. 1 1 1 Throughput = images generated total inference time = images per forward pass inference time per forward pass \mathrm{Throughput}=\frac{\text{images generated}}{\text{total inference time}}=\frac{\text{images per forward pass}}{\text{inference time per forward pass}} . Prior work has made substantial progress by reducing the per-sample cost of diffusion sampling. One line of work reduces the number of denoising evaluations. [ 30 , 31 , 27 , 12 , 13 , 38 , 40 , 39 ] Another line of work reduces the cost of individual denoising evaluations through feature reuse or caching. [ 14 , 8 ] Together, these approaches have substantially improved the efficiency–quality trade-off of diffusion sampling in practice. Despite these advances, further acceleration along the same per-sample axis is increasingly difficult. As denoising evaluations decrease, each remaining step must approximate more of the trajectory, making the dynamics more sensitive to approximation error. [ 34 , 35 ] Caching methods reuse intermediate features across adjacent timesteps, but wider cache intervals amplify mismatch from fully recomputed trajectories. [ 14 ] When the two approaches are combined, reduced-step sampling makes each update more consequential while caching supplies features from increasingly mismatched trajectory states, limiting further gains without additional quality loss overall. Figure 1: Illustration of the ManiFusion framework. K × B K\times B inputs is fused into B B representations, jointly processed by a shared denoising backbone, then unfused via the unfusion module into K K representations per group, and finally passed through a projection layer to produce K K outputs. As gains along the per-sample axis approach saturation, we instead increase throughput by processing more samples within each denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion , a lightweight framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion processes multiple samples within a shared denoising backbone by fusing their representations before the backbone and separating them afterward through index-conditioned unfusion. Specifically, ManiFusion realizes multi-sample computation through Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which uses larger fusion factors in stable regions and smaller factors in sensitive stages. However, generating multiple samples through a single fused representation presents a nontrivial challenge. Each sample needs a distinct denoising prediction, yet fusion combines their states into a representation the size of a single input. Naive superposition can entangle their information [ 37 , 33 ] and compromise the denoising dynamics governing their individual generation trajectories. [ 30 , 9 ] We examine how shared computation can preserve these distinct predictions through a geometric perspective under the manifold hypothesis. [ 20 , 28 , 1 , 2 ] Low-dimensional data structure provides room for samples to coexist, while denoising requires their prediction targets to remain recoverable. Our analysis relates fusion-induced information loss to prediction error, supported by empirical studies of sample separation and denoising behavior. To demonstrate that ManiFusion generalizes across diverse generative settings, we validate ManiFusion across major diffusion model families, including pixel-space U-Nets, diffusion transformers, and latent diffusion models. [ 24 , 22 , 23 ] Our experiments cover both unconditional and conditional generation across broad resolution ranges from CIFAR-10 to ImageNet. We further show that ManiFusion composes naturally with existing acceleration methods, including step-reduction samplers and caching-based acceleration. [ 12 , 31 , 14 ] By operating along a different throughput axis, ManiFusion reaches higher-throughput regimes beyond trajectory shortening or per-step acceleration alone. 2 Method We propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. Since multi-sample generation requires jointly processing multiple trajectories while preserving sample-wise prediction targets, we first establish ManiFusion through dual-space inference (Sec. 2.1 ). In this framework, multiple denoising evaluations are replaced by a single fused computation followed by index-conditioned recovery. We then extend ManiFusion across diverse diffusion backbones and sampling paradigms through Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically allocates the fusion factor according to trajectory dynamics (Sec. 2.2 ). Finally, we develop a geometric intuition for why shared computation can support distinct generation trajectories and what information fusion must preserve to make this possible (Sec. 2.3 ). 2.1 ManiFusion ManiFusion enables multiple samples to share computation through fusion into a common representation and unfusion into individual outputs. Our goal is to validate ManiFusion as a general computational restructuring principle that operates across diverse generative settings, rather than a technique specialized to a particular pretrained foundation model stack. We therefore evaluate ManiFusion across major diffusion model families spanning different denoising spaces, backbone architectures, and conditional generation settings. For pixel-space U-Nets, we apply MF-UNet to DDPM [ 5 ] on CIFAR-10 and CelebA. For pixel-space transformers and conditional generation, we evaluate MF-DiT on class-conditional DiT [ 22 ] on CIFAR-10. For latent-space autoencoders, we apply MF-AE to LDM [ 23 ] on CelebA-HQ. Finally, for latent-space transformers and conditional generation, we evaluate MF-DiT on ImageNet using DiT [ 22 ] . These experiments demonstrate that ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion model families rather than specific architectures, scaling across resolutions, denoising spaces, and conditioning regimes. Experimental settings. All throughput measurements are conducted using batched inference for vanilla baselines and ManiFusion under identical inference environments, including sufficiently large batch configurations, scheduler settings, and hardware setup, to ensure fair comparison. Throughput is reported using end-to-end wall-clock generation time, and computational overhead is evaluated using parameter count and multiply–accumulate operations (MACs). Unless otherwise specified, all ManiFusion results use fusion factors up to K=4, and all models are trained from scratch without finetuning or freezing. Additional details and ablations appear in the appendix. 3.1 Application to Baseline Models We first evaluate ManiFusion on baseline diffusion models, where it achieves nearly 2 × \times throughput while maintaining sample quality close to the baseline without materially increasing model complexity(Tab. 1 ). Qualitative results in the Appendix confirm preserved perceptual fidelity and diversity. We observe similar behavior in transformer-based diffusion models. Interestingly, mixing different class conditions within fused groups is more stable than grouping identical classes, as verified by additional experiments in the Appendix. This supports the interpretation that conditional diversity provides cues for slot separation (Appendix C ). We extend ManiFusion to latent diffusion in two ways. On CelebA-HQ, we apply MF-AE to LDM(Tab. 3 ). We also implement MF-UNet directly on the LDM backbone, with results provided in the Appendix. Empirically, MF-AE exhibits smaller quality degradation than MF-UNet at the same fusion level. This comparison highlights the role of where the shared bottleneck is introduced. MF-AE learns a representation for joint reconstruction, whereas MF-UNet shares the prediction computation at each denoising step. We further evaluate MF-DiT on ImageNet for large-scale class-conditional generation. These results show strong quality across latent U-Net and transformer backbones in both settings.
